:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ given that $f(x,y) = 3x\ln y + 2ye^x.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+2{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{1}{y}+2{e}^{x}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3x}{y}+2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find $f_{y}(x, y)$ for $f(x, y) = xy^{2} + x^{2}\cos y$.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate term by term:
$$
f_y=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy^2)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2\cos y)=2xy-x^2\sin y.
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot (2x)+y\cdot (1) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =x\cdot 1+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the constant multiple rule for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{x}{y}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{y}\cdot (1)-y\cdot \left(-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{y}+\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{x}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x-8{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{y}^{2}) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x)-8{y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂x}(1) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}-0 \\  & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{y}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum rule for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x+3y}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{3y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{3y})+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 3{e}^{3y}+{x}^{2}\cdot 3{y}^{2} \\  & =3{e}^{2x+3y}+3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡y-{3}^{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({3}^{x}\cdot {3}^{y}) \\  & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡y)-{3}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({3}^{y}) \\  & ={x}^{3}\cdot \operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡y-{3}^{x}\cdot {3}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & ={x}^{3}\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡y-{3}^{x+y}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y)-2\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =5\cdot (0)-2\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{x}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{4}}+6xy\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{4}}\right)+\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+6y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+6y\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{y}^{4}}+6y\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{x}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(8x{y}^{4}+\frac{3{y}^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8x{y}^{4})+\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{3{y}^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\right) \\  & =8{y}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+3{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}\right) \\  & =8{y}^{4}\cdot 1+3{y}^{2}\cdot \left(-\frac{4}{{x}^{5}}\right) \\  & =8{y}^{4}-\frac{12{y}^{2}}{{x}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{y}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{x}) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y})+{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =x\cdot {e}^{y}+{e}^{x}\cdot 1 \\  & =x{e}^{y}+{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3\operatorname{arctan}⁡y-x{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3\operatorname{arctan}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡y)-x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{1+{y}^{2}}-x\cdot 2y \\  & =\frac{3}{1+{y}^{2}}-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{x}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(8 y^{4} \sin{\left(x \right)}+4 y \arctan{\left(x \right)}- \frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8 y^{4} \sin{\left(x \right)})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(4 y \arctan{\left(x \right)})-\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right) \\  & =8 y^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sin{\left(x \right)})+4 y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\arctan{\left(x \right)})-y^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right) \\  & =8 y^{4}\cdot \cos{\left(x \right)}+4 y\cdot \frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}-y^{2}\cdot \left(- \frac{2}{x^{3}}\right) \\  & =8 y^{4} \cos{\left(x \right)} + \frac{4 y}{x^{2} + 1} + \frac{2 y^{2}}{x^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=3 x^{4} \ln{\left(y \right)}+2 x e^{y}- \frac{9 x^{2}}{y^{2}}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The notation ${f}_{y}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(3 x^{4} \ln{\left(y \right)}+2 x e^{y}- \frac{9 x^{2}}{y^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3 x^{4} \ln{\left(y \right)})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2 x e^{y})-\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{9 x^{2}}{y^{2}}\right) \\  & =3 x^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\ln{\left(y \right)})+2 x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{y})-9 x^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{1}{y^{2}}\right) \\  & =3 x^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{y}+2 x\cdot e^{y}-9 x^{2}\cdot \left(- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\right) \\  & =\frac{3 x^{4}}{y} + \frac{18 x^{2}}{y^{3}} + 2 x e^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=9 x^{4} \ln{\left(y \right)}+6 x e^{y}- \frac{6 x^{2}}{y^{4}}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The notation ${f}_{y}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(9 x^{4} \ln{\left(y \right)}+6 x e^{y}- \frac{6 x^{2}}{y^{4}}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9 x^{4} \ln{\left(y \right)})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6 x e^{y})-\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{6 x^{2}}{y^{4}}\right) \\  & =9 x^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\ln{\left(y \right)})+6 x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{y})-6 x^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{1}{y^{4}}\right) \\  & =9 x^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{y}+6 x\cdot e^{y}-6 x^{2}\cdot \left(- \frac{4}{y^{5}}\right) \\  & =\frac{9 x^{4}}{y} + \frac{24 x^{2}}{y^{5}} + 6 x e^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{x}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(3 y^{4} \ln{\left(x \right)}+4 y e^{x}- \frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3 y^{4} \ln{\left(x \right)})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(4 y e^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right) \\  & =3 y^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\ln{\left(x \right)})+4 y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(e^{x})-y^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right) \\  & =3 y^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{x}+4 y\cdot e^{x}-y^{2}\cdot \left(- \frac{2}{x^{3}}\right) \\  & =4 y e^{x} + \frac{3 y^{4}}{x} + \frac{2 y^{2}}{x^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $$
\displaystyle f(x,y)=8 x^{4} \sin{\left(y \right)}+9 x \arctan{\left(y \right)}- \frac{3 x^{2}}{y^{3}}.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The notation ${f}_{y}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(8 x^{4} \sin{\left(y \right)}+9 x \arctan{\left(y \right)}- \frac{3 x^{2}}{y^{3}}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8 x^{4} \sin{\left(y \right)})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(9 x \arctan{\left(y \right)})-\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{3 x^{2}}{y^{3}}\right) \\  & =8 x^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sin{\left(y \right)})+9 x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\arctan{\left(y \right)})-3 x^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{1}{y^{3}}\right) \\  & =8 x^{4}\cdot \cos{\left(y \right)}+9 x\cdot \frac{1}{y^{2} + 1}-3 x^{2}\cdot \left(- \frac{3}{y^{4}}\right) \\  & =8 x^{4} \cos{\left(y \right)} + \frac{9 x^{2}}{y^{4}} + \frac{9 x}{y^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

The notation $f_x$ means the partial derivative with respect to $x$. Hold $y$ constant, so $e^{2y}$ and $y^2$ are constant multipliers. First write $e^{3x+2y}=e^{2y}e^{3x}$.

Using the sum and constant multiple rules,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(e^{2y}e^{3x})+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2y^2) \\
&=e^{2y}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(e^{3x})+y^2\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2) \\
&=e^{2y}\cdot 3e^{3x}+y^2\cdot 2x \\
&=3e^{3x+2y}+2xy^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
The factor $3$ comes from differentiating $e^{3x}$; the held factor $e^{2y}$ is unchanged.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find $f_y(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=x\ln y+y\ln x+e^{2x+y}+\dfrac{x}{y}$, where $x>0$ and $y>0$.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The notation $f_y$ means the partial derivative with respect to $y$. Treat $x$ as constant throughout. In particular, $\ln x$ is a constant multiplier in $y\ln x$, whereas $\ln y$ must be differentiated in $x\ln y$.

Rewrite $e^{2x+y}=e^{2x}e^y$ and $x/y=xy^{-1}$ to expose the constant multipliers. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)
&=x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\ln y)
  +\ln x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y) \\
&\quad +e^{2x}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(e^y)
  +x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^{-1}) \\
&=x\cdot\frac{1}{y}+\ln x\cdot 1+e^{2x}\cdot e^y+x\cdot(-y^{-2}) \\
&=\frac{x}{y}+\ln x+e^{2x+y}-\frac{x}{y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here $x$ survives as a multiplier in the first and last terms. The last term is negative because the derivative of $y^{-1}$ is $-y^{-2}$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ given that $f(x,y)=x^2\cos y+y^3.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant. Thus $\cos y$ is a constant multiplier, and the entire term $y^3$ is constant.

Using the sum and constant multiple rules,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2\cos y)+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(y^3) \\
&=\cos y\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2)+0 \\
&=\cos y\cdot 2x+0 \\
&=2x\cos y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(x e^{y}) &=x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{y}) \\
&=x\cdot \left(e^{y}\right) \\
&=x e^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y e^{x}) &=e^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\
&=e^{x}\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=x e^{y} + e^{x}$.

Differentiate with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2 x e^{y}) &=2 e^{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\
&=2 e^{y}\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=2 e^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y e^{x}) &=y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(e^{x}) \\
&=y\cdot \left(e^{x}\right) \\
&=y e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{x}(x,y)=y e^{x} + 2 e^{y}$.

Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(3 x \arcsin{\left(y \right)}) &=3 x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\arcsin{\left(y \right)}) \\
&=3 x\cdot \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{- y^{2} + 1}}\right) \\
&=\frac{3 x}{\sqrt{- y^{2} + 1}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(3 x^{2}) &=3 x^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1) \\
&=3 x^{2}\cdot \left(0\right) \\
&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=\frac{3 x}{\sqrt{- y^{2} + 1}}$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find $f_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=- y^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}+2 y e^{x}$, where $x>0$.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(- y^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}) &=- \ln{\left(x \right)}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y^{3}) \\
&=- \ln{\left(x \right)}\cdot \left(3 y^{2}\right) \\
&=- 3 y^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(2 y e^{x}) &=2 e^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\
&=2 e^{x}\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=2 e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=- 3 y^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)} + 2 e^{x}$.

Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(- 2 y \arcsin{\left(x \right)}) &=- 2 \arcsin{\left(x \right)}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\
&=- 2 \arcsin{\left(x \right)}\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=- 2 \arcsin{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(- 3 y^{2}) &=-3\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y^{2}) \\
&=-3\cdot \left(2 y\right) \\
&=- 6 y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{y}(x,y)=- 6 y - 2 \arcsin{\left(x \right)}$.

:knowledge-point/title: Finding Partial Derivatives of Two-Variable Functions
